title: Pricing by hours per project for Pet grooming
audience: Groomers who write quotes for dogs and cats by size and coat type, and need a price that covers cost and earns a margin.
learningOutcomes: Calculate a cost per productive hour from the owner's own figures
Estimate project hours, including set-up, travel and checking time
Build a quote from hours, a rate and a margin, and state its basis and exclusions

instruction.heading: Why hours are the starting unit
instruction.body: A groom takes longer than the time the animal spends on the table. It includes set-up, the bath, drying, clipping, finishing, the owner's notes and the clean-down. Coat condition changes the time: a matted or heavily shedding coat can take much longer than a clean coat of the same size. Airtasker notes that costs can double for larger thick-coated breeds, so size alone does not capture the cost (last updated 17 March 2025). Start from hours so that the cost of a difficult coat is visible before you quote.

instruction.heading: Build the cost per productive hour
instruction.body: Add the year's total costs: rent or a salon share, van running costs for a mobile groomer, insurance, equipment and blade servicing, shampoo and consumables, booking software, phone, any registration fee that applies, and admin. If you employ a groomer, add wages with on-costs such as leave and superannuation, and check which award or enterprise agreement applies. Divide by productive hours: hours with an animal on the table or in the van, not the open diary. For a mobile groomer, count drive time as a separate cost, not as a productive hour.

instruction.heading: Estimate the hours by size and coat
instruction.body: Estimate the time for each service at a standard speed, by size band (small, medium and large, the bands vendor price guides use), and add a coat allowance for matting, de-shedding or a long coat. Add set-up, clean-down, travel and a checking allowance as named lines. Xero's small-business guide suggests 10 to 20 per cent for unexpected work (Xero Australia, 3 September 2026). That is a general figure, so size your own allowance from records. Record actual minutes after each groom and use the gap to correct the next estimate (Carters Trade Leader, a New Zealand publisher, 1 October 2025).

instruction.heading: Turn hours into a price
instruction.body: Multiply the productive hours by the cost per productive hour, add a margin that reflects the risk (a difficult coat or an anxious animal), and apply your minimum charge. Vendor ranges show the spread. Airtasker lists a medium full clip at $85 to $100 and a large one at $100 to $120 (17 March 2025). Hepper lists a medium full summer cut at $90 and an XL at $120 (5 January 2026). Use these as market checks, not as your price. A price above the range can be correct if your cost base supports it, and you should be able to explain why.

instruction.heading: Keep the quote honest
instruction.body: A quote states the size and coat, the service, the add-ons, the exclusions (for example, a matted coat that needs extra time), what the owner must provide, and how long the quote is valid. Price extra time for a matted coat as its own line, and state the rate before the groom starts. Hepper lists about $10 for each extra 10 minutes of matted-coat work, a vendor figure (5 January 2026). Re-quote when the size, coat or service changes.

instruction.heading: Review your estimates
instruction.body: Compare estimated and actual minutes for the first ten grooms of each size and coat type. Change the standard time, the coat allowance or the margin when the gap is consistent.

procedure: Gather the year's business costs and the productive grooming hours in the same period.
Divide total costs by productive hours to get the cost per productive hour, and count drive time separately for a mobile service.
Set standard times for each size band and service, and add a coat allowance.
Add set-up, clean-down, travel and checking time as named lines.
Multiply the hours by the cost per productive hour, add the margin for risk, and apply the minimum charge.
Write the quote with size, coat, add-ons, exclusions, owner duties and validity, then record actual minutes after each groom.

workedExamples.situation: Illustrative figures only, not market rates. A mobile groomer in Victoria quotes a medium-coated dog for a full clip. The estimate is 1.5 hours with the animal on the table, including set-up and clean-down, plus 1 hour of drive time for the visit, which she counts as a separate cost. Her cost per productive hour is $45 (illustrative), her drive-time cost is $30 an hour (illustrative), and her target margin on price is 25 per cent (illustrative).
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the price for the groom, and what changes if the coat is matted and takes 30 minutes longer?
workedExamples.reasoning: The groom costs 1.5 hours multiplied by $45, which is $67.50. The drive costs 1 hour multiplied by $30, which is $30.00, so the total cost is $97.50. A 25 per cent margin on price means the price is the cost divided by 0.75, which gives $130.00. If the coat is matted and takes 30 minutes longer, the extra cost is $22.50, the total cost becomes $120.00, and the price becomes $160.00, but only if her quote and her matting rule allow the extra time to be charged. The vendor range for a medium full clip is $85 to $100 (Airtasker, 17 March 2025), so her price sits above it. That is acceptable only if her cost base, including the mobile drive, supports it, and she should be able to explain why.

equipmentAndPpe: Quote worksheet by size band and coat type
Time log for each groom, with estimated and actual minutes
PPE as listed on your own safety checklist

commonErrors.error: Pricing from shampoo and clipper costs alone
commonErrors.prevention: Include the van or salon, premises, insurance, equipment, consumables and admin in the cost per productive hour.

commonErrors.error: Counting open-diary hours as productive hours
commonErrors.prevention: Use the hours an animal is on the table or in the van only.

commonErrors.error: Leaving out drive time for a mobile service
commonErrors.prevention: Add drive time as a named line on each visit.

commonErrors.error: Quoting a coat with no line for matting or extra time
commonErrors.prevention: State the extra-time rate and when it applies before the groom starts.

commonErrors.error: Never comparing estimated and actual minutes
commonErrors.prevention: Record actual minutes after each groom, and review the variance monthly.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Pricing guidance only. The Australian Consumer Law applies to pricing statements, and the ACCC says misleading price statements are prohibited (15 July 2026). State and territory rules also apply and differ.
Pay rates, allowances and on-costs for employees may be set by an award or enterprise agreement. Check which one applies before using any wage figure. This lesson does not state those rates.

Mobile grooming rules differ. The ACT code says its principles apply at clients' homes. The NSW code is written for establishments, and its status is not confirmed. Victorian grooming rules were not found and remain UNRESOLVED. Check the rule for each place you work before you set a mobile price.
Hepper is a vendor and affiliate publisher, and its own page conflicts on its XL price. Airtasker is also a vendor. Neither is a regulator's rate.

qualityStandard: Each quote shows size, coat, add-ons, exclusions, owner duties and validity.
The cost per productive hour is calculated from the groomer's own records and dated.
Actual minutes are recorded for the first ten grooms of each size and coat type and compared with the estimate.
No quote is issued without a margin decision and a minimum-charge check.
documentationEvidence: Cost per productive hour worksheet, dated, with the source of each figure
Quote showing size, coat, exclusions and validity
Groom time log with estimated and actual minutes
summary: Start every groom quote from hours, with size and coat as named inputs.
Cost per productive hour uses time on the table or in the van, not the diary.
Matting, drive time and clean-down are named lines, not hidden extras.
Compare estimates with actual minutes, and change the method when they diverge.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which costs belong in the cost per productive hour for a groomer?
options: Only the price the owner pays for the groom, plus any tip
The average price of other groomers in the suburb
Only the wage of the lowest-paid groomer and nothing else
Rent or salon share, van, insurance, equipment, consumables, admin and on-costs, divided by productive hours

knowledgeChecks.question: A medium groom is estimated at 1.5 hours and takes 2.25. What is the right response?
options: Record the actual minutes, find the cause, and adjust the estimate and future quotes
Leave the estimate, since the owner has paid and the dog has gone home
Reduce the time for the next dog and skip the clean-down
Raise the price for this owner only and no one else is charged more

knowledgeChecks.question: Why does a grooming quote need a line for coat condition and exclusions?
options: To hide the margin from the owner
To show what the price covers, so extra time can be priced and disputes are reduced
To make the groom seem smaller than it is
